newsitem.title: LESOTHO: Lesotho seen needing closer links with South Africa.
newsitem.headline: Lesotho seen needing closer links with South Africa.

text.p: Lesotho should improve relations with its powerful South African neighbour to bring about political stability and economic growth in the small kingdom, diplomats say.

Lesotho, with a population of two million people, is bordered on all sides by South Africa and has little to export apart from labour and its abundant water which it sells to South Africa's industries.
The European Union, which previously channelled its aid to try and reduce Lesotho's dependence on South Africa, now believes the kingdom should work with its neighbour.

"We now say it is no use for Lesotho to go it alone, and instead of fighting against it we now emphasise that they should work towards intelligent economic integration in the region and with South Africa," EU representative in Lesotho Jochem Zuidberg told Reuters.
"Such a move would contribute towards political stability and a more responsible government," he added.

"To become wholly independent would become a self-defeating exercise. Lesotho cannot rely on donors for eternity," he said, adding that the EU donated on average more than 100 million rand ($44 million) a year to Lesotho in grants.

Lesotho, which is roughly the size of Belgium, receives over half its revenue from tariffs raised by the Southern African Customs Union and another 40 percent from remittances raised by its nationals working in South African mines.
Lesotho imports 90 percent of its needs from South Africa and its maloti currency is pegged to the South African rand.
A water transfer scheme, the Lesotho Highlands Project, to pump water from Lesotho's mountains to South Africa's industrial heartland of Gauteng will generate about $55 million a year for Lesotho.
Although Lesotho is heavily dependent on South Africa, some diplomats believe its government is too weak in negotiating better deals with South Africa's post-apartheid government.
"The Lesotho government has never had the wisdom to sit down with the South African government and properly discuss its relations with the new South Africa," one diplomat said.

The small landlocked country has been the focus of attention of South African President Nelson Mandela and his counterparts from Zimbabwe, Botswana and Mozambique after an 11-day police mutiny which threatened its government.

The Lesotho government ordered its army to flush out the group of rebels hiding in the national police headquarters demanding amnesty for eight policemen accused of the murder of three colleagues in 1995.
Diplomats said years of political instability in Lesotho scared off foreign investor interest and cast doubts on the ruling Basotho Congress Party's ability to govern.
"The biggest problem Lesotho has in attracting foreign investment is the continual political instability in government and its lack of real control over the security forces," a Western diplomat said.
Unemployment in Lesotho is around 45 percent. Lesotho Chamber of Commerce and Industry's head Makalo Khiba said government ministers were not paying enough attention to developing the economy.
"With the current setup in government I don't see us getting anywhere. There is strife in the ruling party and we don't know where we are going.
"Nobody in government is concentrating on economic development because they are too busy concentrating on the power struggle within the party," Khiba told Reuters.

The extent of poverty in Lesotho is evident just a few minutes drive from the capital Maseru. Small unpainted brick homes clutter a narrow road riddled with potholes which carries an endless stream of dilapidated minibus taxis.
U.S. ambassador to Lesotho Bismarck Myrick said Lesotho should take advantage of the attention being paid to South Africa's young democracy.
"But they will need the internal political climate to change to facilitate this," Myrick said.
